title: Agent Fundamentals
description: What makes a system an agent: the loop, tools, memory and when to stop.

questions.prompt: What best distinguishes an AI agent from a single LLM call?

options.text: It uses a larger model
It always has a graphical interface
It runs a loop where the model chooses actions, observes results and decides what to do next
It never needs a system prompt

questions.explanation: An agent repeatedly plans, acts (often via tools) and observes outcomes. A single call produces one response with no feedback loop.

questions.prompt: In an agent loop, what is an "observation"?

options.text: The result returned to the model after it takes an action, such as a tool output
The user's first message
The model's hidden reasoning
A log line written for developers only

questions.explanation: Observations are the feedback the environment gives the agent after an action. They are what lets the agent correct course.

questions.prompt: Why should an agent have an explicit stopping condition or step budget?

options.text: To make responses longer
Because models cannot call tools more than once
It is only needed for streaming responses
To prevent runaway loops that waste cost and time when the goal cannot be reached

questions.explanation: Without a budget or clear done-criteria, an agent can loop indefinitely. Step limits, timeouts and success checks keep it bounded.

questions.prompt: Which is the most reasonable use of short-term memory (the context window) in an agent?

options.text: Storing every past user across all sessions
Holding the current task, recent tool results and the plan in progress
Saving API keys for later calls
Caching the model weights

questions.explanation: The context window is working memory for the current task. Long-lived facts belong in external storage that is retrieved when relevant.

questions.prompt: When is a simple, deterministic workflow usually a better choice than an autonomous agent?

options.text: When the task is open-ended research
When the steps are known in advance and rarely change
When the user wants creativity
Never; agents are always better

questions.explanation: If the path is predictable, a fixed workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Reach for agent autonomy when the steps genuinely depend on what is discovered along the way.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a "human-in-the-loop" checkpoint?

options.text: To slow the agent down on purpose
To replace the model with a human
To collect training data automatically
To let a person approve high-impact or irreversible actions before they happen

questions.explanation: Checkpoints put a human decision in front of risky actions like payments, deletions or sending messages, where a mistake would be costly.
